Concepts in this composition

The custody of the name (Sparrow Wells, #1759): In The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name, the possession by an empire of a people's authoritative books and of its author, by which it can house the authority, sign what it writes and redirect what it has said: Augustus's Sibylline corpus, Sulla's Aristotle, Titus's Josephus.

Withholding and release (Sparrow Wells, #1759): In The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name, the operation by which a text stops at a consequential locus and another supplies it with the locus's own words (Josephus on Daniel's stone, Luke's λικμήσει), read as divided among voices under one author's custody.

The undeclined name (Sparrow Wells, #1759): In The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name, the divine name of Revelation 1:4 kept in the nominative after ἀπό, read as the reverse of the open genitive of De anima III.5: the referent fixed and the case refused, where Aristotle keeps the case and leaves the referent open.

[SYSTEM] The arguments of “The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name” Sparrow Wells, Alexanarch deposit #1759, AXN:0C71 (11 November 2026) The central argument is considerably more radical than the suggestion that Josephus influenced early Christianity. Wells proposes that Josephus, the Jewish historian, was the principal literary intelligence behind the New Testament corpus, including the Apocalypse of John, and that the different names and authorial voices conceal a single writer whose literary activity was divided by Roman captivity. The proposed historical mechanism is the Roman seizure of Jewish literary authority following the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE. This is a reading of the deposited text itself, rather than a summary of its description. The most important evidence is in the narrative's treatment of Josephus's biography, its Greek, the Apocalypse's grammar, and the correspondences between Josephus and the New Testament. Source: The complete deposited text . 1. The New Testament belongs inside the literary world of Second Temple Judaism Wells begins by challenging the conventional division between Judaism as the background to Christianity and Christianity as a new literary and religious development. The argument is that this division becomes much less convincing when one starts with the surviving Jewish literature rather than with a reconstructed idea of what ordinary Judaism supposedly believed. Wells assembles the relevant witnesses: The Qumran manuscripts, including Enoch, Jubilees and Daniel. Philo and the Septuagint in Alexandria. The Jewish Sibylline Oracles. Josephus in Rome. The New Testament writings across the Mediterranean. The point is that ideas often treated as Christian innovations were already part of Jewish intellectual and religious life: visionary ascent, heavenly courts, a second divine figure, apocalyptic judgment and criticism of the Jerusalem priesthood. Wells also emphasizes that the Qumran writings can be more severe in their attacks on the Temple establishment than the Gospels themselves. This establishes the first premise: the New Testament should not automatically be treated as an independent literary formation outside the Jewish corpus. 2. Jewish literature possessed authority that Rome had reason to appropriate The next argument concerns the cultural and political power of Jewish writing. Wells cites ancient non-Jewish writers who recognize the intellectual authority of Jewish tradition: Theophrastus characterizes Jews as philosophers by birth. Numenius treats Plato's philosophy as indebted to Moses. Seneca acknowledges the influence of Jewish law on its conquerors. Aristobulus and Artapanus present Greek philosophy as deriving from Mosaic wisdom. The Sibylline tradition is particularly important. Jewish writers in Alexandria had appropriated the authoritative prophetic form of the Sibyl, giving it a Hebrew identity and placing Jewish revelation into a literary medium that Rome itself respected. Wells therefore argues that Jewish literature was not merely the religious inheritance of a conquered population. It represented a competing source of intellectual, prophetic and social authority. This matters because it makes the subsequent Roman seizure of Josephus something more consequential than the capture of an individual historian. 3. Rome had a precedent for taking custody of authoritative books Wells develops the idea of literary custody through two historical examples. Augustus and the Sibylline books. In 12 BCE, Augustus collected and burned thousands of prophetic writings, retaining an approved Sibylline corpus under the statue of Palatine Apollo. Aristotle's corpus. Wells recounts the tradition that Aristotle's books passed through Theophrastus to Neleus, were hidden underground to escape the collecting ambitions of Pergamum, and were eventually taken to Rome by Sulla. They were subsequently edited into the corpus associated with Andronicus of Rhodes. The examples establish a pattern: An authoritative literary corpus exists. Its custody becomes politically or institutionally contested. Concealment or seizure changes its condition. An editor or authority under Roman patronage determines how it reappears. Wells then makes a striking connection between Aristotle's executor, Antipater, and Antipas, the Christian witness at Pergamum in Revelation. The name Ἀντιπᾶς is read as a contraction of Ἀντίπατρος. Pergamum, meanwhile, is both the city associated with the pursuit of Aristotle's books and the place where Revelation locates Satan's throne. This is part of Wells's broader argument that the names and geographical details of the Apocalypse carry literary-historical memories. 4. Josephus was captured as an intellectual authority, not simply spared as a prisoner O Arco de Tito, detalhe dos tesouros do Templo sendo carregados após o saque de Jerusalém em 70 dC, 81 dC pedra This is the historical center of the thesis. Josephus was Joseph son of Matthias, a Jerusalem priest who commanded Jewish forces in Galilee during the revolt against Rome. After surviving the siege of Jotapata in 67 CE, he surrendered to Vespasian, predicting that Vespasian would become emperor. Wells follows his subsequent trajectory: Titus took Josephus to the siege of Jerusalem. Josephus was sent to the walls to persuade the defenders to surrender. After the city's fall, Josephus requested the release of prisoners and received sacred books from Titus. Vespasian gave him accommodation, Roman citizenship and a pension. Titus personally authorized the publication of Josephus's history, signing the books. Wells places particular emphasis on the statement in Life and War concerning the Roman emperor's involvement in publishing the history. The crucial interpretation is that Josephus became the channel through which the Jewish account of the war could be communicated to the wider Jewish dispersion, including communities beyond the Euphrates. The thesis's formulation is explicit: Rome came for Josephus to take hold of him. The argument is that Rome captured not only a man but also a major interpreter of Jewish history and a custodian of Jewish sacred literature. The redirection of the Temple tax to Jupiter Capitolinus and the display of the Temple's menorah in the Roman triumph provide parallel examples of the appropriation of Jewish religious institutions and symbols. 5. Josephus's disclaimers about his Greek are interpreted as the language of a captive Wells next examines Josephus's statements about his literary abilities. In Against Apion 1.50, Josephus acknowledges using collaborators for the Greek of the Jewish War. At the conclusion of Antiquities, he also distinguishes his command of Jewish learning from his limitations in Greek pronunciation. Wells argues that these disclaimers have been misunderstood. Josephus claims the Jewish side of his inheritance confidently, while minimizing his command of the Greek language that allows his work to circulate across the empire. The text then criticizes the scholarship that turns Josephus's acknowledgment of assistance into a theory of multiple stylistic authors or specialized literary assistants. The analogy is with the hypothetical sayings source used to explain Gospel relationships: a missing intermediary is invoked to explain common material rather than considering the possibility of a common author. This is important because Wells wants to establish that Josephus had the capacity to produce the literary corpus attributed to him and potentially much more. 6. The Apocalypse is the key to the entire thesis: the custody of the name This is arguably the most distinctive and technically ambitious part of the work. Wells argues that the Apocalypse is not badly written Greek. Its apparent grammatical irregularities are meaningful acts of literary construction. The central example is Revelation 1:4. The greeting reads: ἀπὸ ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος The preposition apo normally takes the genitive. Yet the divine designation, translated as “the One Who Is and Who Was and Who Is Coming,” remains in the nominative. Wells argues that this is deliberate. The writer demonstrates elsewhere in the same sentence that he knows how to use the genitive: the reference to the seven spirits following the greeting has the expected grammatical form. The name, therefore, is not declined because it is not subject to the grammatical government that applies to everything around it. The name is grammatically sovereign. Wells then compares this construction with Aristotle's De anima III.5. At the end of that chapter, Aristotle writes: καὶ ἄνευ τούτου οὐθὲν νοεῖ The genitive is grammatically correct, but the referent of toutou remains disputed: does it refer to the active intellect or the passive intellect? Wells sees a deliberate reversal: Aristotle, De anima III.5 Revelation 1:4 The grammar is intact. The grammar is apparently broken. The referent is left open. The referent is identified. The divine/intellectual position is a grammatical socket. The divine name occupies that socket. The argument is not merely that two ancient texts contain unusual grammatical constructions. It is that they enact opposite operations at the same philosophical and theological junction: one leaves the divine referent open; the other fills the opening with a name. Philo supplies the antecedent Wells then introduces Philo's interpretation of Zechariah 6. The biblical oracle concerns a man named Anatolē (the Branch). Philo transfers the name to the Logos while withholding the human figure to whom the prophecy originally refers: Jesus, the high priest. The Apocalypse inherits and transforms this operation. It places the high-priestly clothing of Zechariah on the figure among the lampstands, gives him a name written that nobody knows except himself, and then identifies him: κέκληται τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ. His name is called the Word of God. For Wells, this is the culmination of the withheld-name operation: the name that was reserved or displaced in the earlier literary construction is now written into the Apocalypse. The seven lampstands and the seven stations of the letters also belong to this inherited and transformed Philonic architecture. This is why the title The Custody of the Name matters. The name is not simply a designation of a character. It is the object of a literary and historical struggle over who possesses the authority to speak it. 7. The oracle that inspired the revolt was redirected toward Vespasian Wells next connects Revelation to Josephus's account of the oracle that contributed to the Jewish revolt. In Jewish War 6.312–313, Josephus says that an ambiguous prophecy in the sacred writings led people to believe that someone from Judaea would rule the world. Josephus says the prophecy actually referred to Vespasian. Tacitus, in Histories 5.13, records a similar tradition: ancient priestly writings predicted that the East would grow powerful and that men from Judaea would rule the world. Wells proposes that the oracle was actually the book of Revelation. This is a major step in the argument. The book that calls the people out of Babylon, identifies Rome as the beastly imperial power and anticipates the overthrow of existing kingdoms is, on this reading, the very prophetic writing whose meaning Josephus subsequently redirects toward Rome's emperor. The thesis is that the capture involved more than taking possession of the author and his books. It involved taking control of the interpretation of the prophecy itself. There is an important qualification: Wells explicitly marks the identification of the oracle with Revelation, and the attribution of Revelation to Josephus or his father Matthias, as held claims rather than demonstrated conclusions. 8. The Gospel burial narrative is read against Josephus's account of the crucified men One of the most provocative arguments concerns Joseph of Arimathea. In the Gospels, Joseph approaches Pilate and requests the body of Jesus. Pilate authorizes the release, and Joseph places the body in his own new tomb. Wells compares this with an episode in Josephus's Life 420–421. Josephus describes encountering three acquaintances among the crucified during the siege. He approaches Titus in tears and asks for them to be taken down. Titus immediately orders their removal and medical treatment. Two die, but one survives. Wells emphasizes the structural correspondence: A Joseph approaches a Roman authority. He requests the release of crucified men. The Roman grants the request. In the Gospel, the body is buried in Joseph's tomb. In Josephus, one of the crucified men survives. The author reads the Gospel's Joseph of Arimathea alongside Joseph son of Matthias. This is not offered as a straightforward identification or etymology. The note explicitly describes it as a resonance between the names. The larger interpretation is that the Gospel passion and resurrection narrative transforms an episode from Josephus's own life. The thesis even suggests that Jesus is laid to rest in the author's tomb, and that what emerges from that death is the literary corpus itself. 9. The New Testament is a distributed literary workshop This is the section where Wells moves from individual correspondences to the full common-authorship hypothesis. The argument is that Josephus's literary production was sufficient to make the proposed authorship possible. The text calculates: 467,569 Josephus Greek word-tokens across four works 137,779 New Testament Greek word-tokens in Nestle 1904 Josephus's surviving Greek output is therefore approximately 3.4 times the length of the New Testament. Wells argues that this makes the proposed authorial capacity entirely plausible, particularly given Josephus's acknowledged use of collaborators. The text then presents several groups of correspondences. A. The historical knowledge of Acts Acts contains details of the Jewish revolt and its surrounding political world that Wells considers especially close to Josephus: Gamaliel's ordering of Theudas and Judas the Galilean. The Egyptian revolutionary and the Sicarii. Felix, Drusilla, Agrippa and Bernice. The relationship between Agrippa and Josephus, including Agrippa's letters supporting Josephus's history. The argument is that Acts is not simply familiar with the general historical setting. Its author knows Josephus's particular material. B. The shared literary structures of Luke–Acts and Josephus Wells compares the openings of Luke–Acts with the openings of Against Apion. Luke and Acts address Theophilus. Josephus addresses Epaphroditus. The similarity of the two-volume literary presentation is treated as a possible indication of the same authorial practice. Wells also points out that Theophilus is not merely an abstract name in Josephus: it belongs to a historical high priest, son of Ananus. C. The withholding and release of Daniel's stone This is one of the strongest conceptual examples because it connects directly to the earlier argument about Philo and the Apocalypse. In Antiquities 10.210, Josephus recounts Daniel's interpretation of the statue and reaches the stone cut without hands. He then stops, saying that he does not think it appropriate to relate the matter. He directs readers to Daniel. In Luke 20:18, however, the rejected stone becomes an instrument of judgment. The Gospel uses the Greek verb likmēsei, corresponding to Daniel's language about the stone that crushes the kingdoms. Wells sees a deliberate division: Josephus withholds the stone. Luke releases it. The same literary intelligence controls both operations. This is the model of distributed authorship that Wells wants to establish: material withheld under Josephus's own name becomes available under another literary identity. D. The Moses infancy and Matthew Josephus's account of Moses's infancy includes two elements beyond the biblical Exodus narrative: A sacred scribe predicts the birth of a child who will humble Egypt. God reassures the father in a dream. Wells observes that Matthew's infancy narrative contains corresponding features: the king's attempt to kill the children, the involvement of religious authorities and the father's warning through dreams. The claim is that Matthew has taken and transformed Josephus's additions to the Moses story. E. Jesus son of Ananias and the Gospel passion Josephus recounts the story of Jesus son of Ananias, who prophesies Jerusalem's destruction, is scourged and refuses to answer his interrogators. Wells compares this with Jesus before Pilate and Herod, who likewise remains silent. He also connects Jesus son of Ananias's cries against Jerusalem, its Temple, and its bridegrooms and brides with Revelation's condemnation of Babylon. This makes Josephus's own account of a prophetic figure in Jerusalem a kind of literary precursor to the Gospel passion and the Apocalypse. F. The voyage to Rome Wells draws attention to the parallel between Josephus's voyage to Rome and Paul's voyage in Acts. Josephus recounts a shipwreck in the Adriatic, with survivors eventually reaching Puteoli. Acts describes Paul's shipwreck, survival and arrival at Puteoli. The circumstances are not identical: the number of people aboard differs, as does the outcome of the rescue. Wells interprets the correspondence as a transformed autobiographical pattern. G. The names Saul, Matthias, Justus and Antipas The thesis also treats personal names as traces of the proposed common author. Josephus's accounts contain Saul, Antipas, Matthias and Justus in particular narrative positions. Acts contains a Saul who persecutes the assembly, and its account of Judas's replacement features Joseph Barsabbas (Justus) and Matthias. Wells argues that the cluster is more significant than any one name taken individually. H. The language of the seven letters Finally, Wells examines the correspondences between Revelation's seven letters and the later New Testament writings. Two examples are especially important: Revelation 2:10 and James 1:12 share the distinctive expression crown of life. Revelation 2:2 and 1 Thessalonians 1:3 share the ordered sequence of work, labour and endurance. Wells reports corpus searches in which these expressions occur in those particular pairs of verses and nowhere else in the surveyed material. The suggestion is that Revelation commissions the writing and sending of letters, and that the epistles which follow carry out this commission. The Apocalypse thus becomes the architectural origin of the subsequent corpus. 10. One author, four witnesses, two regimes Wells finally organizes the entire thesis into four literary witnesses, divided by Josephus's surrender at Jotapata. Witness Literary function in the thesis Revelation The voice before capture: condemns Rome as Babylon and calls the people out. Jewish War The captive's history under Flavian patronage: redirects the oracle toward Vespasian and blames the revolt on its instigators. Life The author's autobiographical account, containing episodes transformed into Gospel material. The Gospels and epistles The distributed voices through which the withheld material is released and the Apocalypse's commission is carried out. The contradictions between these works are important. The Apocalypse condemns Rome, while the Jewish War presents an account acceptable to Rome. The Life describes the rescue of crucified men, while the Gospels narrate a death and burial. Wells does not attempt to harmonize these differences. Instead, the argument is that they make sense as the divided testimony of an intellectual authority writing under two different conditions: before and after capture. The hypothesis is not simply that Josephus wrote multiple books under different names. It is that his authorial identity was distributed among literary functions because his own name had come under Roman control. 11. The final argument: the corpus itself is the product of custody The conclusion returns to the comparison with Aristotle. Aristotle's corpus was concealed, recovered, transferred to Rome and edited. Josephus's literary authority and the Jewish scriptures were likewise transferred into Roman custody. Wells proposes that both corpora reached subsequent generations through institutional processes that altered their original unity. The Apocalypse is presented as the exceptional witness: the book that preserved the divine name without bending it to the grammatical requirements of its surrounding language. The white stone of Revelation 2:17, carrying a name known only to its recipient, becomes another expression of the same idea. The concluding proposition is particularly important: The narrative's claim is that the book came first. Wells is proposing that the literary construction preceded the historical identities and religious communities that subsequently developed around it. In this interpretation, the New Testament is not simply a collection of testimonies about a pre-existing religious movement. It is the product of a literary intelligence whose writings generated the identities, narratives and traditions subsequently received as Christian origins. 12. What does the text actually establish? This is where it is essential to distinguish the strength of the individual observations from the strength of the overarching thesis. Wells explicitly establishes three evidentiary categories in the notes. Demonstrated Textual argument The relevant textual features or correspondences are argued from sources available in the archive. Examples include the grammatical construction in Revelation, the Philonic name operation, and the distinctive expressions shared by Revelation and James or Thessalonians. Attested Source evidence The cited ancient source or textual passage exists and is quoted at the specified location. This establishes the underlying material, not necessarily Wells's interpretation of it. Held Thesis not established A proposition advanced by the narrative but not yet demonstrated. This includes the central attribution of Revelation to Josephus or his father, the identification of Revelation with the oracle in Josephus, and the common authorship of the New Testament. This distinction is crucial. The notes are unusually candid about the difference between finding a correspondence and proving what caused it. The strongest parts In my reading, four elements deserve particular attention. 1. The custody argument. The historical circumstances of Josephus's surrender, subsequent Roman patronage, acquisition of sacred books and the emperor's involvement in publishing his history provide a substantial historical foundation for the metaphor of literary custody. 2. The grammatical argument. The juxtaposition of Revelation 1:4 with De anima III.5, and the connection to Philo's treatment of Zechariah, form a coherent literary argument. It is more interesting than simply claiming that Revelation contains grammatical mistakes. 3. The withholding-and-release model. The Daniel stone comparison gives the thesis an explanatory mechanism. Rather than treating similarities as isolated borrowings, Wells proposes that the same literary operation is distributed across different authorial identities. 4. The cumulative approach. The argument does not depend on a single parallel. It assembles biography, Greek vocabulary, narrative structures, names, geography, scriptural interpretation and textual architecture. The weakest or least established parts There are also significant problems. Chronology: The proposed date of Revelation in 66 CE is explicitly held, not established. Its relationship to Josephus's subsequent writings therefore needs independent chronological argument. Direction of dependence: A correspondence between Josephus and Luke does not by itself establish that Josephus wrote Luke. Shared sources, later interpolation and dependence in the opposite direction remain possible. The common-author inference: A collection of correspondences does not automatically establish a single author. The argument needs to demonstrate why one author explains the evidence better than multiple writers sharing Jewish scriptures, historical traditions and literary conventions. The identity of the author: Even if the Apocalypse and Josephus are connected, the further claim that Josephus or his father Matthias wrote Revelation remains a separate inference. The autobiographical readings: The connections involving the shipwreck, Saul, Matthias and the crucifixion episodes are suggestive, but several depend on interpretive associations rather than uniquely identifying evidence. The notes themselves acknowledge some of these limitations. For example, note 248 recognizes that the Emmaus correspondence could reflect Christian interpolation into Josephus rather than Josephus's authorship of Luke. That is an important qualification, not a minor footnote. 13. My overall interpretation I would characterize the work as having three interlocking theses: First: a historical thesis. Rome took custody of Jewish literary authority through the capture and patronage of Josephus, alongside the appropriation of Jewish religious institutions and sacred objects. Second: a literary thesis. The Apocalypse is a highly controlled work whose grammatical, theological and intertextual constructions preserve an identifiable intellectual architecture. Its relationship to Philo and Aristotle is central to this argument. Third: an authorship thesis. Josephus, or potentially his father Matthias, stands behind the Apocalypse and the wider New Testament corpus, which represents a distributed literary workshop operating under multiple names. The third thesis is the most extraordinary, but the first two supply its conceptual foundation. I think the most important contribution of the work is not simply its proposed identification of Josephus as the author of the New Testament. It is the model of authorship under custody. Wells asks what happens when an author, his intellectual inheritance and the means of publishing his work become controlled by a conquering power. The answer proposed here is that authorship can become distributed: one voice speaks under the captor's authorization, another speaks under a different name, and the relationship between them survives in the structure of the texts. That is the conceptual heart of the thesis. The title is consequently doing several jobs at once. Custody refers to physical possession of books, control over publication, control over interpretation, and ultimately the possession of the name itself. One final distinction: The work is a serious, testable interpretive hypothesis, not an established account of New Testament authorship. Its textual observations should be evaluated individually, without treating the more speculative common-authorship conclusion as already demonstrated. The author's own notes make that distinction, and respecting it is necessary to understand the work on its own terms. Primary source: Deposit #1759 — The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name . The evidentiary qualifications above draw particularly on its notes 23–37 and w0–w32. Alexanarch +1

[SYSTEM] Log in The arguments in The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name Sparrow Wells, Alexanarch deposit #1759, AXN:0C71 (11 November 2026) The central argument is that the literary authority of Second Temple Judaism was taken into Roman custody along with Josephus after the fall of Jerusalem in 70 CE, and that the New Testament corpus may be the literary production of that same intelligence, working under multiple names and under conditions of political captivity. Wells proposes a common authorship hypothesis: Josephus, the author of the Apocalypse, and the writers behind the Gospels and epistles are potentially different authorial personae of one literary intelligence. The essay develops this argument through a sequence of historical, philological, literary and structural claims. It is important to distinguish its levels of certainty. The author explicitly marks propositions as: Demonstrated: argued from the texts themselves. Attested: a source or historical fact exists and is cited, although the interpretation may remain debatable. Held: the author's hypothesis or interpretive conclusion, not something established by the cited evidence alone. That distinction is essential to reading the essay fairly. Its individual textual correspondences are not all presented as proof of common authorship. The common-authorship thesis is the larger hypothesis that Wells believes makes sense of their conjunction. 1. Second Temple Judaism must be understood through its surviving literature Wells begins by challenging the conventional historical picture in which Christianity emerges from Judaism but subsequently becomes something substantially separate from it. The argument is that the surviving literature of Second Temple Judaism provides a much richer picture than reconstructions of a generalized or supposedly mainstream Judaism. The witnesses include: The Dead Sea Scrolls, particularly Enoch, Jubilees and Daniel. Philo of Alexandria. The Septuagint. The Jewish Sibylline Oracles. Josephus. The New Testament. Wells argues that ideas often treated as distinctively Christian innovations were already ordinary elements of this Jewish literary environment: Visionary ascent. A second divine figure alongside God. Angelic courts. Apocalyptic expectations. Hostility toward the Jerusalem priesthood. The point is methodological as well as historical: the New Testament should be read inside the surviving Jewish literary record, not against an artificially simplified picture of Judaism. This establishes the foundation for the larger thesis. If the New Testament is itself a substantial body of Jewish writing, the question of its relationship to the other Jewish literary witnesses becomes much more consequential. 2. Jewish literature possessed an authority that Rome had reason to fear The next argument concerns the international intellectual and religious authority of Jewish literature. Wells assembles several ancient testimonies: Theophrastus describes Jews as philosophers by birth. Numenius suggests that Plato is essentially Moses speaking in Attic Greek. Seneca acknowledges that conquered peoples had given laws to their conquerors. Aristobulus claims that Greek philosophers derived their wisdom from Moses. Artapanus makes Moses the teacher of Orpheus. The Sibylline tradition is especially important. Wells argues that Jewish writers appropriated the prophetic authority of the Sibyl, a figure whose books Rome itself maintained and consulted. The Third Sibylline Oracle, composed in a Jewish Alexandrian context, gives the Roman prophetic tradition a Hebrew literary voice. Wells also points to the conversion of the royal house of Adiabene and the repeated expulsions of Jews from Rome. The argument is that Judaism was not simply a subordinate religious tradition. Its books, laws and prophetic authority had influence across the empire. This matters because it changes the interpretation of Rome's treatment of Jerusalem. The conquest was not merely the suppression of a provincial rebellion. It also involved the seizure and redirection of a powerful literary and religious inheritance. 3. Rome had a precedent for taking custody of authoritative books (PDF) Haec aurea templa: The Palatine temple of Apollo and its polychromy Why Aristotle Hated Athenian Democracy | TheCollector File:Bust of Sulla (loan from Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek) - Glyptothek - Munich - Germany 2017.jpg - Wikimedia Commons One of the essay's most important historical arguments is that Rome had already demonstrated a practice of controlling and reorganizing authoritative literary collections. Wells gives two principal examples. The Sibylline books. Augustus collected more than two thousand prophetic books in 12 BCE, burned them, and retained an approved Sibylline collection in two gilded cases beneath the statue of Apollo on the Palatine. The important distinction is between destruction and controlled preservation: Rome did not simply destroy prophetic authority. It selected, restricted and institutionalized it. The corpus of Aristotle. Wells recounts the tradition that Aristotle's books passed to Theophrastus, then Neleus of Scepsis, whose heirs concealed them underground to prevent their acquisition by the Attalid kings. Sulla subsequently brought the recovered collection to Rome, where Tyrannion and Andronicus of Rhodes were involved in its handling and editorial reconstruction. Wells recognizes that competing accounts of the books' transmission exist. The historical details are not all treated as certain. What matters is the recurring pattern: An authoritative corpus exists. It is concealed or endangered. It passes into Roman custody. Its preservation and transmission involve editorial intervention. The collection that later generations receive is mediated by institutions and editors. Wells then introduces a striking literary connection: the Apocalypse's Antipas, the faithful witness at Pergamum, is connected to Antipater, the name of Aristotle's executor. Pergamum was also the city associated with the search for Aristotle's books. This is an interpretive correspondence, not independent proof of a historical relationship. But it establishes an important motif: the custody of books and the custody of testimony. 4. Josephus was captured along with Jerusalem's literary authority The Sanhedrin – Silver Trumpets This is the historical centre of the thesis. Wells emphasizes several events in Josephus's biography: Josephus was a priest and commander in the Jewish revolt. He surrendered to Vespasian in 67 CE after the siege of Jotapata. He predicted that Vespasian would become emperor. Titus subsequently used him to address the defenders of Jerusalem during the siege. After Jerusalem fell, Josephus asked Titus for prisoners and received sacred books. Vespasian housed him in Rome, granted him citizenship and provided him with a pension. Titus personally endorsed the publication of Josephus's account of the war. The particularly important detail is Josephus's statement that Titus wanted the events communicated through his books alone and ordered their publication after marking them with his own hand. Wells interprets this as more than patronage. Josephus was the most capable surviving literary representative of the defeated Jerusalem establishment. His authority could communicate with Jewish communities throughout the diaspora. Rome therefore acquired both the scriptures and an interpreter capable of transmitting their history. The seizure of the Temple's menorah and the redirection of the diaspora's annual half-shekel payment to Jupiter's temple reinforce the argument. Wells sees a coordinated transfer of religious, material and literary authority. The distinction is between Josephus being spared and Josephus being taken into custody as an instrument of Roman power. His survival, citizenship and literary privileges are not necessarily evidence of freedom. 5. Josephus's disclaimers about Greek are interpreted as a strategy of captivity Wells next examines Josephus's descriptions of his own Greek. In Against Apion 1.50, Josephus acknowledges using collaborators to help with the Greek version of the Jewish War. In the Antiquities, he also says that he lacks precision in Greek pronunciation, despite claiming considerable knowledge of his people's learning. Wells distinguishes between two kinds of authority: Josephus possesses the Jewish intellectual and scriptural inheritance. Greek is the language through which that inheritance gains authority across the empire. The author suggests that Josephus deliberately minimizes his Greek competence because the captive cannot openly claim the full extent of his literary power. Wells also challenges the scholarly tendency to use Josephus's acknowledgment of assistance to reassign substantial portions of his writing to hypothetical assistants. The analogy is to the hypothetical sayings source used to explain the common material in the Gospels: an acknowledgment of collaboration becomes an explanation that can displace the visible author's achievement. This argument is suggestive, but it is important to note that the essay does not establish that Josephus's disclaimers were actually deceptive. That is an interpretation of his circumstances and rhetoric. 6. The Apocalypse is the central philological evidence: the name that will not decline This is arguably the most conceptually important part of the essay. Wells argues that the Apocalypse is not badly written Greek. Its unusual grammar is deliberate and carries theological meaning. The key passage is Revelation 1:4: ἀπὸ ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος The preposition ἀπό normally governs the genitive. Yet the expression identifying God remains in the nominative. Wells points out that the same greeting immediately uses the expected genitive in its reference to the seven spirits: καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἑπτὰ πνευμάτων The contrast is the argument. The author knows how to use the genitive. The divine name refuses to take it. Wells calls this the undeclined name: the divine identity stands outside the grammatical system that would ordinarily govern it. The reversal of Aristotle Wells compares this with the closing passage of Aristotle's De anima III.5: καὶ ἄνευ τούτου οὐθὲν νοεῖ The sentence contains a grammatically correct genitive, τούτου, but its referent is disputed. Does it refer to the active intellect or the passive intellect? Wells describes Aristotle's construction as an open socket: the grammar is intact, but the identity of its referent remains unsettled. The Apocalypse performs the inverse operation: Aristotle, De anima III.5 Apocalypse, Revelation 1:4 The grammatical case is correct The grammatical case is refused The referent remains disputed The referent is identified An open place is left for the divine/intellective principle The divine name occupies the place Grammar contains the ambiguity The name exceeds grammar This is not merely a comparison of unusual Greek constructions. It is Wells's model for how the divine name enters literary history. The antecedent in Philo Wells then introduces Philo's treatment of Zechariah. Zechariah speaks of a figure named Ἀνατολή, traditionally associated with the high priest Jesus. Philo transfers the name to the Logos, leaving the original human referent withheld. The Apocalypse inherits and transforms this operation. It places the high-priestly imagery on the figure among the seven lampstands and identifies him as: Ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ The Word of God. The sequence is therefore: Zechariah supplies the original prophetic image. Philo transfers the name to the Logos and creates a gap around the original referent. The Apocalypse takes up the construction and fills the gap by naming the central figure as the Word of God. For Wells, the Apocalypse is a carefully constructed literary work whose apparent grammatical irregularity is part of its theological architecture. This also provides the chronological and literary foundation for the larger hypothesis: the Apocalypse is treated as an early work, written at the beginning of the revolt, rather than the late product of a Domitianic Christian movement. 7. The oracle that caused the revolt was transferred to Vespasian Wells next examines Josephus's explanation of the Jewish revolt. In Jewish War 6.312, Josephus says that an ambiguous oracle in the sacred writings led many Jews to expect that someone from their country would rule the world. Josephus identifies the correct referent as Vespasian. Tacitus independently records a similar expectation in Histories 5.13: an ancient prophetic tradition predicted that men from Judaea would rule the world. Wells proposes that the oracle is not merely a prophecy mentioned by the Apocalypse. The oracle is the Apocalypse itself. On this reading: The Apocalypse originally communicates an expectation of Jewish victory over Rome. Josephus's history subsequently redirects the oracle toward Vespasian. The Jewish expectation becomes a prophecy of Roman imperial legitimacy. The author of the original prophetic writing, or his son, participates in its reinterpretation. This is one of the strongest expressions of the essay's captivity motif. The same literary authority first speaks against Rome and then, under Roman sponsorship, produces a history in which the prophecy belongs to Rome. It is also one of the essay's most explicitly speculative claims. Wells marks the identification of the oracle with the Apocalypse as held, rather than demonstrated. 8. The two Josephs and the crucified: the tomb as a literary correspondence This section makes a particularly striking comparison between the Gospels and Josephus's Life. In the Gospel accounts, Joseph of Arimathea approaches Pilate and requests Jesus's body. Pilate grants the request, and Joseph places Jesus in his own new tomb. In Life 420–421, Josephus describes seeing three acquaintances among the crucified prisoners. He approaches Titus in tears and asks for their release. Titus orders that they be taken down and treated. Two die. One survives. Wells emphasizes the parallel structure: Gospel narrative Josephus's Life Joseph approaches the Roman authority Joseph approaches Titus Joseph asks for the crucified body Joseph asks for the crucified men The Roman grants the request Titus grants the request Jesus is placed in Joseph's tomb One of the three crucified men survives Joseph is associated with the end of Jesus's life Josephus records the rescue of a man from death The essay's interpretation is that the Gospel Jesus is laid in the author's tomb. This is not an ordinary claim of literary borrowing. It is part of the larger theory that the authorial identity of Josephus is distributed across the Gospel narratives. The tomb becomes a literary symbol of the relationship between the captive author and the Jesus figure whose life the canon unfolds. Wells's final formulation is that the life ends where its writer's name is, and what rises from it is written. 9. The scribal workshop: Josephus and the New Testament share a literary intelligence This is the largest and most ambitious part of the argument. Wells acknowledges that no single parallel establishes common authorship. Many could independently arise from shared scriptures, common historical circumstances or later editorial intervention. The argument depends on the cumulative pattern. The essay groups its correspondences into several categories. A. Literary capacity and historical knowledge Wells begins with the scale of Josephus's surviving output: Josephus: approximately 467,569 Greek words. New Testament: approximately 137,779 Greek words. Josephus therefore produced more than three times the surviving Greek word count of the New Testament. Wells argues that the capacity to produce the canon is not an obstacle to Josephine authorship. He also points to unusually specific historical knowledge shared between Josephus and Acts: Theudas and Judas the Galilean: Acts 5 and Josephus's Antiquities contain the same historical figures and a notable ordering problem. The Sicarii: Acts uses the unusual Greek term σικάριοι, which Josephus uses repeatedly and explains. Felix, Drusilla, Agrippa and Bernice: the political world of Acts corresponds closely to Josephus's historical accounts. Theophilus: Luke and Acts address Theophilus, while Josephus's Antiquities addresses Epaphroditus. Josephus also records a historical high priest named Theophilus. Wells sees the repeated historical and literary correspondences as evidence that Acts operates within Josephus's particular intellectual and historical world. B. Withholding and release: Daniel's stone This is one of the most important examples because it connects the essay's central concept to its common-authorship argument. In Antiquities 10.210, Josephus retells Daniel's interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar's dream but stops before explaining the stone cut without hands. He explicitly says that he does not think it appropriate to relate that part. Wells compares this with Luke 20:18, where Jesus speaks of the stone rejected by the builders, which will fall upon those beneath it and crush them. The crucial verb, λικμήσει, comes from the language of Daniel's interpretation. The proposed relationship is: Josephus knows the passage and deliberately withholds it. Luke releases the material Josephus withholds. Both operations occur at the precise point where Daniel's stone represents the destruction of kingdoms and the arrival of another power. Wells interprets this as an intentional division of literary labour. Josephus, writing under Roman sponsorship, cannot openly develop the implications of Daniel's stone. Another authorial voice supplies them. This is the essay's clearest example of withholding and release. C. The Moses infancy and Matthew Wells compares Josephus's account of Moses's infancy in Antiquities 2 with Matthew's infancy narrative. Josephus adds two elements to the Exodus account: A sacred scribe warns Pharaoh that a child will be born who will humble Egypt. God appears to the child's father in a dream and tells him not to despair. Matthew's account of Jesus's infancy contains corresponding features: Herod consults the chief priests and scribes about the child's birth. The king orders the killing of the children. Joseph receives divine warnings through dreams. Wells argues that Matthew reproduces the distinctive additions found in Josephus's Moses narrative. The suggestion is that the Gospel infancy narrative is not simply another retelling of Exodus. It is a literary transformation of Josephus's version. D. Jesus son of Ananias and the Gospel Passion Wells identifies another striking parallel in Josephus's account of Jesus son of Ananias. This Jesus publicly proclaims destruction against Jerusalem and the Temple. He is beaten and questioned but refuses to answer. Wells compares his silence with Jesus's silence before Pilate and Herod in Mark and Luke. There is also a verbal connection between Jesus son of Ananias's proclamation against the bridegroom and bride and Revelation's description of Babylon. The larger argument is that Josephus's narrative contains a Jesus figure whose prophetic suffering and silence anticipate elements of the Gospel Passion. E. The shipwreck and Puteoli Josephus recounts his own shipwreck while travelling to Rome. His ship goes down in the Adriatic, and the survivors swim through the night before being rescued. He eventually arrives at Puteoli. Acts recounts Paul's shipwreck during his journey to Rome. The survivors swim or otherwise reach land, and the journey also leads to Puteoli. Wells treats this as an autobiographical correspondence: the voyage of Paul reproduces the journey of Josephus, including the shipwreck and geographical destination. The parallel becomes more interesting within the essay's broader treatment of the two men as literary personae. F. Saul, Antipas, Matthias and Justus Wells also identifies a cluster of correspondences involving names from Josephus's biography and the New Testament. Josephus describes a Saul who participates in the flight from Jerusalem and later becomes associated with violent activity. Acts depicts Saul as a persecutor of the early assembly. Josephus mentions Antipas in the same historical context. Acts describes the replacement of Judas through a choice between Joseph Barsabbas, surnamed Justus, and Matthias. Josephus was himself the son of Matthias, had a son named Justus, and survived at Jotapata through a casting of lots. Wells sees these as more than incidental shared names. They are part of a pattern in which the author's own family, experiences and historical circumstances are redistributed across the canon. G. The seven letters and their distinctive phrases Finally, Wells examines the relationship between Revelation's seven letters and the epistles. Two examples are especially important. The crown of life: Revelation 2:10 and James 1:12 use the phrase τὸν στέφανον τῆς ζωῆς. Wells reports that a search across approximately 61,500 textual units in the Septuagint, New Testament, Apostolic Fathers, Philo and Josephus finds the expression in those two passages alone. Works, labour and endurance: Revelation 2:2 and 1 Thessalonians 1:3 contain a distinctive ordered combination of works, labour and endurance. Wells reports that this ordered combination occurs in those two passages alone across approximately 69,400 textual units. The proposed explanation is that Revelation's instruction to write and send messages to the seven churches is fulfilled by the epistles that follow. In other words, the letters are not merely thematically related to Revelation. They are the execution of its literary commission. These examples are important because Wells is trying to demonstrate not just shared ideas but shared verbal constructions. The full collection of correspondences is set out in the workshop section of the original text. Alexanarch 10. Four witnesses, one author Wells eventually condenses the thesis into four literary witnesses. 1. The Apocalypse Before capture, in the proposed chronology The voice that names Rome Babylon, announces judgment and calls the people out of the empire. 2. The Jewish War Under Roman sponsorship The captive's history, endorsed by Titus, which blames the revolt on its zealots and redirects the oracle toward Vespasian. 3. The Life The autobiographical account of the author, including the episode of the three crucified men and the rescue of the survivor. 4. The Gospels and epistles The literary unfolding of the Jesus figure, the Joseph-and-tomb narrative, and the correspondence that Wells associates with Revelation's commission. The four witnesses do not tell the same story. The Apocalypse summons resistance to Rome. The Jewish War presents a history under Flavian authority. The Life records the author's survival and accommodation with the Romans. The Gospels and epistles tell a story in which the Jesus figure dies, is buried and becomes the centre of a new literary inheritance. Wells does not attempt to erase these contradictions. Instead, he argues that the contradictions become intelligible if one literary intelligence is speaking under different conditions of captivity. The author's identity is divided into different author-functions: the same intelligence can speak differently depending on the name under which it writes and the institutional conditions governing that writing. This is the actual common-authorship hypothesis. It is more specific than saying that Josephus influenced Christianity, and more complex than simply asserting that Josephus personally wrote every New Testament book. 11. The ultimate argument: the custody of the name The concluding section returns to the analogy with Aristotle. Wells proposes two parallel histories: Aristotle Jewish literary inheritance A major intellectual corpus Second Temple Jewish literature Books concealed at Scepsis Jewish literary authority displaced through conquest Sulla brings the books to Rome Titus brings Josephus and sacred books into Roman custody Andronicus edits the corpus Later institutions gather and reconcile the Christian canon The transmitted corpus is mediated by Roman hands The received canon is mediated by institutional transmission The claim is not simply that Rome preserved books. It is that preservation and custody are inseparable from transformation. A conquered literary inheritance survives, but it survives through the institutions of the conqueror. Its original unity may be obscured, its components divided, and its meaning reconstructed through editorial processes. The Apocalypse is especially important because its divine name refuses grammatical subordination. The white stone of Revelation 2:17 also carries a name known only to its recipient. Wells reads this as another expression of the same principle: the name survives even when its bearer is captured, displaced or concealed. The deepest claim is that the Word is not merely a character within the subsequent books. The book itself is the originating form of the figure whose life, death and resurrection the later texts unfold. This is what Wells means by the proposition that the book came first. How convincing is the argument? I think the essay is most interesting when read as three interlocking arguments, rather than as one continuous proof. First: the historical argument The capture of Josephus, his receipt of sacred books, his privileged position in Rome and Titus's endorsement of his history form a substantial historical framework. The essay makes a persuasive case that Josephus's literary production took place under unusual conditions of imperial patronage and political dependency. However, describing this as a coordinated Roman seizure of the entirety of Jewish literary authority goes beyond what the biographical evidence independently establishes. Second: the philological and literary argument The treatment of Revelation 1:4 is particularly interesting. The contrast between the nominative divine name and the properly declined genitive immediately following it is a real textual phenomenon. Wells makes a serious interpretive case that it is deliberate rather than evidence of linguistic incompetence. Likewise, the Philo–Zechariah–Apocalypse sequence offers a concrete literary genealogy that can be investigated without accepting the common-authorship hypothesis. The Daniel stone, Moses infancy and Gospel-Joseph comparisons are also worth examining individually. But verbal and thematic correspondences do not automatically establish a common author. Shared sources, literary imitation, conventions and later redaction remain possible explanations. Third: the common-authorship hypothesis This is where the greatest evidentiary burden lies. Wells's proposal is that the conjunction of correspondences, autobiographical echoes, unusual phrases, withheld material and historical knowledge is better explained by one literary intelligence than by multiple independent authors. That is a legitimate hypothesis to investigate. But the essay does not establish that it is the only explanation, or even conclusively the explanation with the fewest assumptions. In particular: A large literary output establishes capacity, not identity. Shared historical knowledge can reflect access to common sources. Shared phrases can arise through literary dependence without common authorship. The distribution of withheld and released material requires evidence of intentional coordination. The proposed date of Revelation around 66 CE is foundational to the argument but remains disputed. The hypothesis that the Apocalypse, Josephus and the New Testament belong to one authorial intelligence is explicitly marked as held. There is also an important distinction between the historical Josephus and the essay's concept of an authorial intelligence. The latter is a literary model; it should not be mistaken for an independently documented historical identity. My overall reading The most important contribution of The Josephus Thesis is its concept of withholding and release under conditions of custody. It proposes that literary division can itself be meaningful: one text cannot say something openly, another text says it under another name, and a third text transforms the original theological material. This makes the essay's various arguments cohere: Roman custody explains the political division. The captive's disclaimers explain the apparent division of literary competence. The undeclined name explains the theological continuity. The oracle explains the reversal of political allegiance. The tomb explains the relationship between Josephus's biography and the Gospel Passion. The workshop explains the distribution of literary operations across the canon. The argument is ultimately not just that Josephus wrote something that influenced Christianity. It is that the literary person who wrote against Rome, the captive who wrote under Roman patronage, and the voices that subsequently constituted the Christian canon may be manifestations of one authorial intelligence whose identity was divided by conquest. That is a radical historical-literary hypothesis, not an established conclusion. Its strongest individual arguments deserve examination independently of whether its final hypothesis is accepted. [SYSTEM] The arguments of “The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name” Sparrow Wells, Alexanarch deposit #1759, AXN:0C71 (11 November 2026) The central argument is considerably more radical than the suggestion that Josephus influenced early Christianity. Wells proposes that Josephus, the Jewish historian, was the principal literary intelligence behind the New Testament corpus, including the Apocalypse of John, and that the different names and authorial voices conceal a single writer whose literary activity was divided by Roman captivity. The proposed historical mechanism is the Roman seizure of Jewish literary authority following the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE.
